questions.question: This man golf when a kangaroo bounds up to him, grabs his club and hits his ball half a mile.
questions.explanation: In storytelling and anecdotes, Present Simple and Present Continuous are used to make actions feel immediate and alive. The background context or longer ongoing situation takes the Present Continuous, while the main sudden event takes the Present Simple. Here, playing golf is the ongoing background situation, so Present Continuous is required.

questions.question: She goes up to this man and straight into his eyes.
questions.explanation: When narrating consecutive main events in a story, they are listed using the Present Simple to create a vivid, fast-paced narrative feel. Since the first verb ("goes") is in Present Simple, the sequential action follows in the same tense.

questions.question: He his glasses, so he doesn't recognise her at all.
questions.explanation: A person's temporary physical state or appearance at a specific moment in a story acts as the background context and is expressed using the Present Continuous. Not wearing glasses is a temporary circumstance here.

questions.question: I was in the park reading a newspaper, when all of a sudden this dog at me.
questions.explanation: After words like "suddenly" or "all of a sudden" within a narrative context, the Present Simple is frequently used to highlight a sudden, unexpected interrupting action.

questions.question: So last night, I for the bus when this man walks up to me and starts talking.
questions.explanation: Even when referring to past events (like "last night"), stories told in a live conversational style use the Present Continuous to describe the longer background activity happening when another event interrupts it.

questions.question: Then this woman the door, walks in and sits down without saying a word.
questions.explanation: A chain of consecutive primary actions in a story narrative is linked together using the Present Simple tense.

questions.question: The sun and the birds are singing when the two travellers reach the old cottage.
questions.explanation: Weather conditions and ambient setting descriptions serve as the background atmosphere of a story and are framed in the Present Continuous.

questions.question: King to the left-hand court and Adams makes a wonderful return.
questions.explanation: During live sports commentaries, actions happening right at the moment of speaking are reported using fast, concise Present Simple forms for completed single actions.

questions.question: She magnificent tennis in this match - she has hardly made a mistake.
questions.explanation: In live reporting, an overall temporary state or performance level spanning a specific duration ("in this match") takes the Present Continuous.

questions.question: Ortega passes to Miller, who the ball into the corner of the net!
questions.explanation: Sequential quick actions during a live athletic commentary are narrated consecutively using the Present Simple tense.

questions.question: Rodríguez far below his usual level today; he has already lost three service games.
questions.explanation: Temporary conditions describing how someone is performing on a specific day ("today") are appropriately expressed with the Present Continuous.

questions.question: It here that the museum will be closed for two years.
questions.explanation: Fixed expressions used to introduce written information from texts, notices, or signs ("It says here") always take the Present Simple.

questions.question: I you're thinking of moving to Canada - is that true?
questions.explanation: "I hear" is a standard fixed Present Simple phrase used to introduce pieces of news or information gathered from others.

questions.question: Sophia me you're planning to emigrate next year.
questions.explanation: The reporting structure "(Someone) tells me" is standardly utilized in the Present Simple to share updates or news received from a specific person.

questions.question: I from your message that the deadline has been moved to Friday.
questions.explanation: "I gather" functions as a standard Present Simple expression used to draw conclusions or share understandings derived from messages or communications.

questions.question: I you've been promoted - congratulations!
questions.explanation: "I understand" is a polite, common Present Simple formula used to acknowledge or report information previously learned or heard.

questions.question: They the new bridge will open some time in June.
questions.explanation: "They say" is an impersonal introductory Present Simple phrase used to state general reports or rumors.

questions.question: Headline: FOREIGN MINISTER AFTER ELECTION DEFEAT
questions.explanation: News headlines conventionally employ the Present Simple tense to report recent past events vividly and directly.

questions.question: Headline: SECOND QUAKE NORTHERN JAPAN
questions.explanation: Headline style universally relies on the Present Simple to make past occurrences sound current and impactful.

questions.question: Headline: SCIENTISTS ICE ON THE MOON
questions.explanation: Present Simple is the standard grammatical choice for headline writing to announce recent discoveries or findings concisely.

questions.question: At the beginning of the novel, three men a suitcase full of money in a crashed plane.
questions.explanation: When summarizing or recounting the plot of a novel, film, or written work, the Present Simple is standardly used.

questions.question: In the film, Loni Baranski the role of a private detective.
questions.explanation: Descriptions of characters, actor roles, and plots within films or stories require the Present Simple tense because the artistic work exists permanently in that state.

questions.question: In Chapter 6, Thompson a list of the largest European companies.
questions.explanation: Plot references, chapters, and structural details inside a book are described using the Present Simple.

questions.question: You your mind - it's impossible to make any plans with you.
questions.explanation: The pattern "be + constantly/always + -ing" describes excessively frequent habits, often carrying a tone of annoyance or complaint about someone's behavior.

questions.question: She her keys - that's the third time this week.
questions.explanation: Using "forever" with the Present Continuous highlights a repeated, irritating habit that frustrates the speaker.

questions.question: Was Olivia always you for money when you shared a flat?
questions.explanation: The past continuous version of the annoying habit pattern ("was/were + always/constantly + -ing") requires the gerund (-ing) form of the main verb.

questions.question: At eight o'clock I'm usually to work, so call me on my mobile.
questions.explanation: The Present Continuous can describe regular routines or habits tied to a specific time of day ("At eight o'clock I'm usually driving...").

questions.question: He's always that he has no money, but he's just bought a new car.
questions.explanation: The structure requires an -ing verb form immediately following the "is always" construction used for emphasizing repetitive complaints.

questions.question: He's complaining about the food, which is very irritating.
questions.explanation: To express irritation over a frequently repeated action within this pattern, focusing adverbs like constantly or always are required, rather than frequency words denoting infrequency (like rarely or hardly ever).

questions.question: Which sentence is NOT possible?

options.text: She's always losing her house keys.
She's always lose her house keys.
She always loses her house keys.

questions.explanation: This option is grammatically impossible because the base form of a verb (lose) cannot directly follow the auxiliary contraction and adverb combination ("She's always..."). It must either take -ing (losing) or an -s inflection (loses) depending on the intended tense structure.
